title: 77-kelvin DRAM: crude poly-Si transistors hold charge for hours
idea: Box: MIM charge x solid-phase-crystallized poly-Si TFT (leaky at 300 K) x voltage sense amp x 2D x glass or Si x PECVD a-Si plus furnace crystallization. At 77 K off-current falls by >1e6, so grain-boundary-limited TFTs from a low-mask university flow meet retention for liquid-nitrogen-cooled racks.
why: Uses temperature to relax process quality (no single-crystal Si, no EUV-grade junctions) and nearly removes refresh; LN2 cooling overhead is a few W per W; risk is system-level cryo adoption.
note: Grain-boundary trap-assisted leakage may not fall 1e6 at 77 K; easy university test.

title: Urban-mining line requalifies retired server DRAM
idea: Inverts 'new supply needs new wafers'. Robotic hot-air reflow strips DRAM packages from retired server DIMMs, a 48-hour retention and row-hammer stress screen sorts them, and they are re-mounted on CXL memory-expander cards for pooled tiers.
why: Hundreds of millions of GB retire yearly; recovered supply at ~10-20% of new-wafer capital per GB, zero EUV.
note: CXL reuse of retired DDR4 already pursued by hyperscalers.

title: Certified pre-owned DRAM: re-profiled hyperscaler memory with warranty
idea: Borrowed from certified pre-owned cars: a 10-person shop buys DIMMs from retired cloud servers by the ton, runs 48-hour retention, row-hammer and temperature profiling on FPGA test rigs, rewrites each DIMM's SPD with measured timing and refresh bins, swaps weak chips and sells warrantied modules for CXL memory expanders.
why: Supply: millions of DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs retire yearly; reuse adds supply with zero wafer capacity at ~30-50% of new price.

title: Eliminate the silicon wafer: DRAM on Gen-8.5 display glass panels
idea: Build 12-16 tiers of oxide-TFT gain cells at F~0.5 um on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass in under-used LCD/OLED fabs, which already own panel-scale litho, sputter and PECVD. One panel has ~60x the area of a 300 mm wafer, so even at coarse F it holds ~3-7 TB of capacity-tier memory behind a CXL-style controller.
why: Capital and crucible chokepoint: display-fab capex per m2 is ~50-100x lower than a DRAM fab, with no Czochralski silicon, quartz crucible or EUV; targets ~$1-3/GB for a slower (~100 ns) tier that frees real DRAM for hot data.
note: Idle Gen-8.5 LCD fabs as capacity-tier memory; doubt: 12-16 tier panel yield and defect density at panel scale.

title: Reverse fab: harvest, retest and rebin retired server DRAM
idea: First principle: DRAM has effectively unlimited endurance and no dominant wear-out, so a 5-year-old die is physically almost as good as new. Build automated lines that desolder DRAM packages from retired DIMMs and boards, reball them, run full BIST, retention and row-hammer binning, and assemble certified second-life modules.
why: Supply: hyperscalers retire many exabytes of DRAM per year; recovered bits cost ~5% of new-fab capex per bit and arrive in months.

title: Federated defect-image library compresses new-fab yield ramps
idea: Worse: every new fab learns its defects alone over 2-3 years. Flip: entrants and toolmakers feed inline SEM/optical defect images and parametric fails into a standardized defect taxonomy. Classifiers train federated (data never leaves each fab) and ship root-cause models and recipe corrections to new lines on day one.
why: Capital: ramp months burn depreciation (~55% of wafer cost); cutting the ramp from ~24 to ~10 months saves ~$1B+ per new fab.

title: Laser interference gratings plus coarse cuts define the whole array
idea: Worse: insist that every array layer needs a $200M scanner and a custom reticle. Flip: expose the purely periodic wordline/bitline layers with maskless two-beam 193 nm immersion interference lithography (a ~$10-20M tool), pitch-split by SAQP, then trim with one low-resolution DUV cut mask. Arrays need periodicity, not arbitrary shapes.
why: Capital intensity: array litho tool cost drops ~10x and array masks shrink to cut layers only.

title: Substitute global bitline sensing with local gain transistors from same VCT step
idea: Split each bitline into 16-cell segments; each segment's charge drives the gate of a local gain transistor made in the same vertical-channel-transistor step as the cells (no extra mask), which pulls a ~50 mV current-mode signal onto the global bitline. With a ~1 fF local line, the cell needs only ~1 fF, so the capacitor can be shallow.
why: Constraint: 50 mV global swing instead of ~0.5 V plus 5x smaller cell charge gives ~10-20x less bitline energy per access; facet: capacitor AR from ~70:1 to ~15:1 (fact 1).
note: Segment-local gain lets ~1 fF cells and shallow capacitors; doubt: gain-transistor Vt mismatch vs 50 mV signal.

title: IBM eDRAM trench sold as merchant pre-capacitored substrate wafers
idea: IBM's deep-trench eDRAM died when its single in-house SOI process ended with GlobalFoundries' 7 nm exit. Disaggregate it: a substrate vendor (Soitec-style) mass-produces blank wafers with a uniform grid of deep-trench capacitors, and any fab, including U.S. legacy logic fabs, builds access transistors and periphery on top aligned to that grid.
why: Capital: moves the deepest etch and high-k module into one specialized high-throughput substrate fab; lets non-memory fabs make DRAM-class memory; ~30% of DRAM process steps outsourced to a shared, fully utilized line.
note: Lets logic fabs build DRAM-class memory on a pre-made cap grid; density stays at eDRAM levels.

title: Hitachi's single-electron grain memory stacked in 64 cheap tiers
idea: Hitachi's room-temperature single-electron memory (Yano, 1990s) stored a few electrons in grains of 3-4 nm polysilicon and died because random grains caused wild threshold scatter. Tame the scatter with per-cell write-verify calibration and a 3-cell majority code, and exploit its simplicity of thin films with no capacitor or deep etch by depositing 64 tiers gated by one shared vertical-gate hole pattern.
why: Meets 100x: tiers are just thin depositions, writes are fast direct tunneling (~10s of ns), retention minutes to hours; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: 3x cell redundancy, calibration time, variability.
note: Thin-film tiers with no capacitor could hit ~$0.1/GB; doubt: grain threshold scatter despite write-verify and 3x redundancy.

title: Open capacitorless memory macro qualified at every U.S. logic fab
idea: Ideal: every fab already in the country is a memory fab. Closest: a CHIPS-funded open PDK macro (gain-cell array, sense amps, refresh controller) qualified on Intel 18A, TSMC Arizona, GlobalFoundries and SkyWater flows, so any U.S. chip can carry hundreds of MB on-die and GB-class stacked working memory without a DRAM fab.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: zero new fab capex; turns logic wafer starts into memory supply and cuts off-chip DRAM demand for caches and KV buffers.

title: Kovio's liquid-silicon ink printed into 32 cheap gain-cell tiers
idea: Kovio printed silicon RFID from liquid cyclopentasilane and folded in 2014 on a tiny market and hard-to-handle pyrophoric ink. Inside a sealed inert coater module, spin 20 nm silicon films from ink, crystallize only the top film with a nanosecond laser, and stack 32 tiers of poly-Si 2T gain cells, each tier patterned by one imprint.
why: Meets 100x: each tier costs a spin, a laser scan and one imprint (~$5-10/wafer) instead of epitaxy or transfer; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: grain-boundary leakage forces ms refresh and defect mapping.
note: Spin-on Si tiers at ~$5-10/wafer each; grain-boundary leakage and ms refresh likely erode DRAM-class value.
